content.text:
A lots of docs were created about the package sync (scope of and implemented in this PR). User requirements were very high level at the start: only what was in issue description of #118 and maybe in another, old, high-level doc that lists all functionalities of pc-switcher. Don't bother searching for it.
Along the way, while responding to your analysis questions and to the many questions that came up during implementation, testing and review (still in progress), the requirements became finer but the decisions we made have spread around a myriad of docs, code comments, ADR, ...
I asked you in another session to reconstruct a user requirements document. This gave "docs/planning/Package sync requirements.md". That's not what I wanted.

So let's take a step back. What is a "user requirements document" for you?
For me, it is NOT a list of 100's of separate rules that are impossible to reconstruct mentally (for a human; I don't know about you but I doubt) into a vision of how the product should do, look like, behave. The 100's of rules written like a lawbook are the conversion of the "user requirements document" into hard rules that the implementation can be checked against.
For me, user requirements are more prose, maybe with diagrams or sketches, that explain the intent of a product and how it should work and behave. Use-cases can be a good way to express (a big) part of user requirements, but not everything can nor should be formulated as use case.
What do you propose as structure and how do we get there? I absolutely want the reconstruct a high level user requirements doc like I describe it, because with all documentation spread over a lot of places and mostly as small individual decisions without a vision of the whole nor of how the individual rules hang together, it has become impossible for me, nor for any reviewer or tester, human or AI agent, to
- understand the product and the logic that we need and decided upon, after all back-and-forth decisions;
- verify if the implementation covers those real user's needs/requests.

I want to be able to review a (rather high-level, but concrete) document that I understand, approve it, and then let a reviewer critically check if the implementation and the tests cover the requirements.

Do you agree? Challenge me if there are points you disagree with or if this is a bad idea anyway.

PS Don't throw away the detailed articles of "docs/planning/Package sync requirements.md" if they are still valuable.

PPS I just glanced through them and spotted immediately a first problem with ambiguous phrasing. A requirements doc should be written in a way that it is clear and unambiguous.
PKG-FR-MACHINE-SPECIFIC: "offered again on that machine. The mark MUST be local to that machine": "THAT" machine is very unclear. What we decided: the decision that something is machine-specific, is noted in a decision file on the machine that holds the "something". This will be often the target machine, even though pc-switcher is launched on the source machine and the question is presented on the source machine and the decision is made on the source machine.
Example: Source machine does not have package P, target machine has package P. The user is asked on the source machine if package P should be removed from the target machine. The user says "skip always". This decision tells that package P is "machine specific" for the target machine, so the decision is stored there.
I'll start by understanding what exists today before proposing a structure.

input.prompt:
In the repo /home/janfr/dev/pc-switcher, I need a map of ALL documentation that carries package-sync requirements or decisions. Do NOT read source code implementation in depth — focus on docs, but note where code comments/docstrings carry decision rationale.

Find and report:
1. `docs/planning/Package sync requirements.md` — read it FULLY. Report its exact structure (all headings, the ID scheme, how many requirement articles, and give me ~5 representative verbatim article texts so I can judge the style). Report total line count.
2. Every other doc under docs/ that touches package sync (apt, snap, flatpak, manual installs, package_sync jobs). List path + one-line description of what decisions it holds. Look in docs/adr/, docs/planning/, docs/dev/, and anywhere else.
3. Any GSD planning artifacts: .planning/ directory — phase dirs for package management sync (Phase 02?), PLAN.md, SPEC.md, RESEARCH.md, UAT/verification docs, REVIEW.md. List them with one-line descriptions.
4. The GitHub issue #118 description — fetch it with `gh issue view 118` and report the full body verbatim.
5. Any UAT / user-acceptance-test docs for this phase (they often encode intended behavior).

Return: a structured inventory (path → what it holds → whether it is authoritative-decisions or derived), plus the verbatim #118 body, plus the full heading outline of `Package sync requirements.md` and the 5 sample articles. Be thorough — breadth matters more than depth here.

In the repo /home/janfr/dev/pc-switcher, I need to understand the ACTUAL user-facing behavior model of package synchronization as implemented on the current branch (gsd/phase-02-package-management-sync).

Explore the package sync implementation and report a coherent narrative of how it behaves from the USER's point of view — not an API listing. Specifically:

1. What managers are covered (apt, snap, flatpak, manual installs?) and where each lives in the source tree.
2. The end-to-end flow of a package sync run: what happens in order, what is compared between source and target, what the user is asked, when.
3. The decision/prompt model: what choices the user gets (install/remove/skip/skip-always/batch...?), what "skip always" means, where those decisions are persisted (file path, on which machine), and how batching works.
4. Direction semantics: is it one-way source→target? What about packages present on target but not source? Repositories/PPAs?
5. Machine-specific marking: how a package gets marked machine-specific, WHICH machine stores that mark, and what file/format.
6. Anything about ordering, dependencies, held packages, versions/revisions, channels.
7. Where "manual installs" (non-package-manager software) fit in.

Report as prose narrative + a list of the key files (path:line) that establish each behavior. I want to be able to write a high-level requirements document from your report, so emphasize INTENT and user-visible behavior over code structure. Be very thorough.

result.output:
1	# PC-switcher
2	
3	A synchronization system for seamless switching between Linux desktop machines (laptops, workstations).
4	
5	## Navigation
6	
7	**Related Documentation:**
8	- [Architecture Decision Records (ADRs)](adr/_index.md) - Architectural decisions with rationale
9	- [Package sync requirements](Package%20sync%20requirements.md) - What "installed packages must sync" requires concretely: `PKG-FR-*` obligations, `PKG-NG-*` non-goals
10	- [Feature Specifications](../specs/) - Feature-level specs, plans, and implementation details
11	  - [001-core](../specs/001-core/) - Core sync engine architecture
12	
13	## Vision
14	
15	Keep pc's in sync with minimal friction. We aim at almost full system-state replication rather than as simple sync of user data.
16	
17	The concrete use case involves two laptops:
18	- **P17** (primary, stationary): Heavy laptop at home, primary work machine
19	- **XPS13** (secondary, mobile): Light laptop for travel, offline capable
20	However, the solution should be generic to support any number of machines.
21	
22	Enable a simple workflow: work on one machine, sync before switching, resume on the other — all without manual file management or real-time cloud syncing overhead.  
23	This must work
24	
25	## Scope Requirements
26	
27	The pc's are mainly used by a single user, with occasional multi-user scenarios (e.g., family members).
28	
29	The machines are used for development (coding, building, testing), general productivity and office work, and occasional multimedia consumption (play music, video).
30	
31	### What Must Sync
32	
33	1. **User data** (`/home`, `/root`)
34	    - All documents, code, configs, application data
35	    - Selective caches: dev tool caches (`uv`, `pip`, `cargo`, `npm`) synced; browser/IDE caches excluded
36	    - Specific mention for VS Code
37	2. **Installed packages**: apt, snap, flatpak, manual .debs, custom PPAs, packages installed through install scripts
38	3. **Application configurations**: All app settings including GNOME Desktop, cloud mounts, systemd services
39	4. **System configurations**: The machine independent `/etc` files, startup services, users/groups, ...
40	5. **File metadata**: Owner, permissions, ACLs, timestamps must be preserved
41	6. **VMs**: KVM/virt-manager VMs
42	7. **Docker**: Images, containers, volumes, cache.
43	8. **k3s**: state of the local single-node k3s cluster, including PVCs
44	
45	### Never Synced: Machine-Specific items
46	
47	- SSH keys (`.ssh/id_*`)
48	- Tailscale config (`.config/tailscale`)
49	- Machine hardware cache (GPU shaders, fontconfig)
50	- Machine-specific packages and configuration
51	
52	## Environment
53	
54	- All machines run Ubuntu 24.04 LTS
55	- Machines must be reachable via SSH during sync (LAN, VPN such as Tailscale, or other network)
56	- All machines have a single btrfs filesystem with a flat layout (all synced data on one filesystem)
57	
58	## Workflow
59	Only one machine is actively used at a time.
60	
61	Simple workflow:
62	1. Work on source machine
63	2. Startup/awaken target machine if not started yet
64	3. Manual trigger sync from source to target
65	4. Wait for sync to complete
66	5. Resume work
67	6. (Optional) Suspend/shutdown source machine
68	
69	### Acceptable Constraints
70	It is acceptable to have some constraints on the environment, on the way the machines are used or on the sync operations, as long as they are clearly documented and do not significantly hinder usability.
71	
72	A few examples:
73	- Way and location to install "bare" packages (manual .debs, install scripts)
74	- Certain applications cannot be running during sync
75	- VMs need to be suspended or powered off before sync
76	- User needs to logout from desktop environment before sync
77	- User needs to execute some commands in a specific program before/after sync
78	- Subvolumes need to be created for certain directories
79	
80	However, everything that can be automated should be automated.
81	
82	### Conflict Detection and Resolution
83	Even though PC-switcher is not designed for concurrent use of source and target machines (no bi-directional sync), it should **detect conflicts** that arise from (unsupported) concurrent use.
84	
85	Conflicts must be reported, but resolution is manual.
86	
87	## UX
88	
89	- Single command to launch the entire sync process and performs all necessary operations on both source and target machine
90	- Simple, intuitive and clear user experience during synchronization and conflict and error handling
91	- Terminal based UI
92	
93	## Project and development principles and attention points
94	More or less in order of importance, but trade-offs are possible:
95	
96	1. Reliability: no data loss, conflict detection, consistent state after sync, detailed logging, ability to audit and roll back changes
97	2. Smooth UX with minimal manual intervention
98	3. Use well-supported tools and best practices where possible
99	4. Minimize disk wear (all disks are NVMe SSDs)
100	5. Sync speed
101	6. Maintainability, simplicity:
102	    - Simple approach and architecture
103	    - Easy to understand, modify and maintain the sync system
104	7. Documentation always up-to-date with the current state of the sync system.  
105	   Documentation on all levels, easily navigable between levels:
106	    - Rationale for decisions
107	    - High level architecture
108	    - Implementation details
109	    - Low-level scripts
110	    - User documentation
111	
112	
113	### Project structure
114	This repository will hold the complete implementation of the sync system:
115	- Scripts and programs implementing the sync logic and workflows
116	- Installation and upgrade script to setup the sync system on the machines, including the installation of dependencies
117	
118	This repository will also hold all documentation:
119	- High-level architecture and design decisions
120	- Implementation details
121	- User documentation and usage instructions
122	- Development guidelines
123	
124	This repository will NOT serve for configuration management. It should be possible for multiple users to use PC-switcher on their own machines with their own configurations.
125	
126	## Ideas for later
127	
128	- Parallel run of sync jobs (e.g. user data and system state in parallel)
129	- Partial sync (e.g. only user data, no system state, skip docker/k3s/VMs)
130	- Machines can be in use in parallel, but only by different users. E.g. User A works on P17, User B on XPS13. Changes will be mainly in user data. For user data, uni-directional sync from one machine to the other is still possible. System state changes on the target machine must be avoided in this mode.
131	- Bi-directional sync with conflict resolution for user data
132	- Bi-directional sync with conflict resolution for system state
133	- Sync over WiFi
134	- Sync (maybe partial) while working on the source machine
135	- GUI / webui (for monitoring sync status, starting sync, making selections, resolving conflicts). Complication: where to host/access the GUI/webui if there is a constraint that the user is logged out of both machines?
136	- Sync over internet
137
